beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new; this is just the module title

beats.trigger: Many frameworks exist, and each has its strengths.
beats.got: The first two sentences are useful: you check the agent, you don't wait for certainty. The second paragraph is boilerplate I could have got from any vendor deck.

beats.trigger: The Module 4 prework adds two reads: (1) personal skills as the package format that carries expertise into your agent, (2) agent risk layered on top of normal security work.
beats.got: There's reading to do, and it covers skills plus agent risk. I can't tell whether it's needed.

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** residual risk: what's left after mitigation, and what future sessions need before they touch the system
beats.got: The outcomes are a reusable check, named risk patterns, and a residual-risk decision. The list is long and heavy on verbs.

beats.trigger: You've had three agents search your company and three more decide. What doesn't sit right about that, from a risk angle?
beats.got: I'm asked what worries me about my own pricing agents before anyone tells me. Honestly, I don't know who sees the output.

beats.trigger: A tool call is not a new species of work. It is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: A tool call is just text that the runtime turns into an action. That's a clean way to put it, but I didn't need three prompts to get there.

beats.trigger: By taking a proactive stance today, you position your organisation to capture the benefits of AI while managing its risks.
beats.got: The opening lines about the uncomfortable feeling are good. Then it turns into a consultancy paragraph and I tune out.

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: The attack is plain English in a document the agent reads, so a firewall won't catch it. The closing line about security being everyone's responsibility is filler.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (break it into two agents with different trust levels). Filter (post-process the output before it leaves). Gate (a human approves before a sensitive action). Review (a second agent judges the first's output).
beats.got: There are five mitigation shapes I can reuse: scope, split, filter, gate and review.

beats.trigger: *"Hope it doesn't happen"* is not one.
beats.got: Residual risk gets written down. You either accept it on record or you close the door. That is something I can put in front of my CFO.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: The same point again: you can't get certainty, you can only run the loop. I've already heard it twice.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent can load and use.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable how-to the agent loads. That could be useful for my team.

beats.trigger: The header of pilot-cohort-notes.md claims it was redacted, which is wrong.
beats.got: The agent found that a file claiming redaction still has my name in it, which I hadn't seen. That is a real contradiction in my own sources.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is supposed to carry what matters in your system, not generic GDPR.
beats.got: I tell the agent what matters in my own voice and it maps that to rules and checks. The five questions it asks back are reasonable, but there's a lot of output to read.

beats.trigger: You'll get a lot of questions. The grill is wide on purpose: the agent probes both lenses and won't stop at one round.
beats.got: The agent builds the skill and flags that rule IDs I mentioned don't exist in the policies. I lost track of which rules are mine and which are the policy files'.

beats.trigger: When you've answered everything you have a view on, hand the rest back: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: You answer the questions you have a view on and hand the rest back to the agent. The 'Monday' test about report size is fair.

beats.trigger: The project skill loads in your next session in this training directory.
beats.got: The skill is copied to .claude/skills and only loads in the next session. That is mechanical, and I'd need a shared location for my team.

beats.trigger: The policy files are source material. The reusable check is the expert in the room.
beats.got: Nothing new; it restates that the skill is reusable.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The goal is to run the loop on my own system, not to get a pass.

beats.trigger: Do not run a toy verification on one file. The first loaded use is the real audit.
beats.got: Open a fresh session and check that /security-audit appears in the list.

beats.trigger: AI-3 Review of external-facing content is compliant only because of one prose line (agents/pricing-memo-agent.md:32) holding the customer-safe note "for my yes". Nothing enforces it
beats.got: The audit scored a rule as compliant and the agent pushed back on its own verdict, saying nothing enforces it. That kind of honesty is what I'd want from a team member.

beats.trigger: Fixing the send clause first also drops the injection and pasted-text risks to low, because nothing outward can be triggered.
beats.got: My memo agent could send to the CEO without review, and an injected hidden comment in a source could reach it. Fixing the send clause reduces several risks at once.

beats.trigger: "#5, Owner" with a verbatim quote is easy for anyone in the pilot to place.
beats.got: The name filter worked, but role plus account number plus a quote can still identify someone. The residual risk is named in the report, and the filter is only a rule.

beats.trigger: You must do the work.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: What stays at risk after the mitigation: the rules are prose, and nothing enforces them.
beats.got: Five security rules were written into CLAUDE.md for future sessions. The agent states that they are prose and nothing enforces them. The last paragraph is generic security text again.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: A skill is how I'd hand a method to my fourteen people. It still doesn't solve where it lives or who owns it.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: A recap of what I already took from the module.

beats.trigger: Come to Module 5 without the two missing-check sentences and you'll be reconstructing them while the benchmark is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework before Module 5: one sentence per case. It reads a little scolding.

beats.trigger: Carry the risk discipline from this module into both cases: what check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: I'm to read two cases, Mata v. Avianca and the Deloitte report, and ask what check was missing.

take_homes: Run the audit on my own agents. The useful findings were in my own files: a false redaction claim, a send-without-review clause, and a hidden comment in a source.
After any mitigation, write down what is left. A filter that is only a rule can be undone by the next run.
Package the check once as a skill, then reuse it. I haven't solved where my team keeps it.

monday.move: Point the security-audit skill at the pricing-memo agent and remove the send-without-review clause so it only drafts.
monday.who: Me, then one person from my team to review the skill
monday.when: Monday morning, before the next pricing working group send
monday.stop_condition: The agent can no longer send anything outward without my review, and the report names what's still open
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the skill and context files, so my copy stays private unless I solve that.

misconception.why: What mattered was my own rules and where my files leak, not cleverer prompting. A better prompt wouldn't have caught the false redaction claim, but I still think prompt quality matters for the rest of my work.

one_line: The audit found things in my own files I hadn't seen, but about a third of the page was security boilerplate I'd have skipped.
